newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: New Australian govt weathers biggest crisis.
newsitem.headline: New Australian govt weathers biggest crisis.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard's new conservative government appears to have weathered its worse political crisis since winning government in March.
In a turbulent week it lost two junior members over alleged conflicts of interests but held on to three senior ministers, including Howard's deputy, despite opposition assaults.
"I can assure you that the events of this week will not be forgotten by quite a number of people," Howard said on radio, referring to ministers whose resignations had been demanded by the opposition.
Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer and Industry Minister John Moore were both accused during the week of share ownership that represented a conflict of interest with their ministerial duties.
Assistant Treasurer Jim Short, responsible for the banking industry, quit on Sunday because he not only held shares in a bank but had granted a banking license to one of its subsidiaries.
Brian Gibson resigned as parliamentary secretary to the treasurer for similar reasons on Tuesday.

But Howard stood by Fischer and Moore and also by Finance Minister John Fahey, who faced the less serious allegation that he had failed to tidy up his share declarations after selling his interest in a company 10 years ago.
Howard said he had angrily reprimanded the ministers.
"I am less than amused at that because they have embarrassed my government and I regret that and I apologise to the Australian people for that having occurred," he said.
"But there has been no evidence of deliberate dishonesty. There's been no evidence of personal gain. There's been no evidence that people have taken a dollar."
Howard's government has had a dream run since it ousted the 13-year-old Labor government.
Even the deficit-slashing budget it announced in August -- the toughest in decades -- was well received by voters convinced that Labor had spent too much money.
Before and after the budget, Howard dominated opposition leader Kim Beazley in opinion polls.

But Beazley found his issue when Moore admitted owning shares in a venture capital company. The company had diverse interests in his own portfolio, such as the computer industry, which benefits from a government bounty.
Fischer held shares in the Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd (BHP), a giant miner and steelmaker whose interests he had to promote as part of his duties as trade minister.
Howard's Liberal-National administration had until now weathered previous crises without losing key members.

Foreign Minister Alexander Downer survived after misleading parliament over foreign reaction to the axeing of an aid programme and Aboriginal Affairs Minister John Herron has survived continued criticism about his handling of his own ultra-sensitive portfolio.
